articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Question: Where the Tourist Tax Money Actually Goes
articles.dek: Bed tax collections hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of TDC expenditures shows millions flowing to projects miles from any beach.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.3 million in tourist development taxes in FY 2025, a 12% increase over the previous year
A Flightline analysis found $8.2 million allocated to projects more than 15 miles from Pensacola Beach, including downtown infrastructure and county-wide marketing
TDC board members defend inland spending as essential to building a 'year-round destination' while some beach-area business owners question whether funds are reaching the tax's primary generators
articles.body:
The money comes from the pillows. Every night a tourist rests their head in Escambia County, 5% of their room rate flows into a dedicated fund controlled by the Tourist Development Council. Last fiscal year, that fund swelled to $47.3 million — more than double what the county collected a decade ago.

Where it goes is another matter.

A Flightline review of TDC expenditure records, board meeting minutes, and grant allocations from fiscal year 2025 reveals a funding landscape that stretches far beyond the beaches generating most of the revenue. Of the $43.1 million disbursed last year, at least $8.2 million — roughly 19% — funded projects located more than 15 miles from Pensacola Beach, the county's primary tourist draw.

The expenditures are legal. Whether they align with the spirit of Florida's tourist development tax statute is a question the TDC board has debated internally for years, according to meeting minutes reviewed by The Flightline.

Following the Money North

The largest single allocation away from the beach: $3.4 million toward the Pensacola Bay Center's ongoing HVAC and seating renovation. The downtown arena hosts concerts, hockey games, and conventions. TDC records classify the spending as 'convention and sports facility improvement,' a permitted use under state law.

Another $2.1 million went to Visit Pensacola's general marketing budget, which promotes the entire county as a destination. Staff salaries, trade show appearances, digital advertising campaigns targeting drive markets in Atlanta, Birmingham, and New Orleans — all funded by bed tax dollars collected predominantly at beach properties.

The Downtown Improvement Board received $890,000 for wayfinding signage, streetscape maintenance, and event support in the Palafox corridor. A $740,000 grant funded archaeological interpretation exhibits at the Presidio site near the foot of the Graffiti Bridge. The Pensacola Little Theatre received $180,000 for facility upgrades. The Five Flags Speedway in Lillian got $95,000 for a regional racing event expected to fill area hotels for one weekend.

None of these allocations violated Florida Statute 125.0104, which governs tourist development taxes. The law permits spending on 'facilities and programs that attract tourists,' a phrase elastic enough to cover nearly any public amenity with a plausible connection to visitor appeal.

The Beach Perspective

Stand at the corner of Via de Luna and Fort Pickens Road on a Saturday in June and the economics are visible. License plates from Louisiana, Alabama, Georgia, Mississippi. Families hauling coolers and umbrellas. Rental cars lined up at Peg Leg Pete's. The beach generates the tax. The question is whether the beach sees enough of it back.

'I pay the tax. My guests pay the tax. Then I watch the money go to fix up Palafox Street,' said Renee Caffey, who manages four rental properties on Pensacola Beach. 'Don't get me wrong — I love downtown. But my parking lot floods every time it rains and the county says there's no money for drainage improvements out here.'

Caffey's complaint is not isolated. The Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce has formally requested a larger share of TDC funds for beach-specific infrastructure in each of the last three budget cycles. Each time, the request has been acknowledged and partially accommodated, but the fundamental allocation formula has not changed.

According to TDC records, Pensacola Beach received $6.8 million in direct infrastructure investment last fiscal year: $3.2 million for ongoing renourishment of the shoreline, $1.9 million for trolley operations and maintenance, $1.1 million for public restroom and beach access improvements, and $600,000 for the Gulfside Pavilion renovation.

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which manages the beach, also receives a separate annual allocation — $4.2 million last year — that falls outside the TDC's direct expenditure accounting. SRIA officials declined to comment on whether they consider the current funding adequate.

The Board's Defense

TDC Chairman David Peacock addressed the geographic spending question at the board's April meeting, according to minutes obtained by The Flightline.

'We are not a beach marketing agency. We are a destination marketing and development organization,' Peacock said. 'Every dollar we invest in making Pensacola a more attractive place to visit — whether that's downtown, whether that's the beach, whether that's Blue Wahoos Stadium — comes back to us in heads on beds.'

Peacock pointed to hotel occupancy data showing growth in downtown Pensacola properties, which he attributed partly to TDC investments in cultural amenities and event recruitment. The Pensacola Grand Hotel and the newly opened Courtyard by Marriott on Garden Street both reported occupancy rates above 70% last year, competitive with beach properties outside peak summer months.

'If you want to build a year-round tourism economy, you cannot put all your eggs in a summer beach basket,' Peacock said. 'We're building a destination that works 12 months a year.'

Visit Pensacola President Darien Schaefer echoed that framing in a written response to questions from The Flightline.

'Our research shows that cultural tourists — visitors who come for museums, history, food, and events — spend more per day and are more likely to return than pure beach visitors,' Schaefer wrote. 'Investing in those assets is not a diversion from our mission. It is our mission.'

What the Law Says

Florida's tourist development tax statute does not require counties to spend bed tax revenue in the geographic areas where it is collected. The law specifies permitted uses: beach renourishment, convention facilities, sports stadiums, tourism promotion, and in some cases, transportation infrastructure. It does not mandate proportional allocation.

Escambia County collects the maximum allowed 5% tax. Of that, 2% must go toward beach renourishment or inlet management under a 2016 statutory revision. The remaining 3% is discretionary within the permitted categories.

The TDC board consists of nine members: four hoteliers (two from the beach, two from the mainland), two elected county commissioners, and three at-large tourism industry representatives appointed by the County Commission. Meeting minutes show that beach hoteliers have periodically pushed for formula changes that would guarantee a larger share of funds for beach infrastructure. Those proposals have not advanced to formal votes.

The Numbers in Context

Pensacola Beach properties account for roughly 62% of the county's total bed tax collections, according to Department of Revenue data analyzed by The Flightline. Downtown and mainland hotels account for approximately 31%. Short-term vacation rentals throughout the county — a growing category — make up the remaining 7%.

If allocations tracked collections proportionally, the beach would receive approximately $26.7 million annually. The actual direct allocation last fiscal year — including SRIA transfers — totaled approximately $11 million, or 41% of what proportional distribution would yield.

TDC staff dispute that framing. They note that beach renourishment projects, which totaled $12.4 million over the last three years, protect the entire tourism economy. They also argue that marketing campaigns benefiting all properties cannot be geographically apportioned.

'You can't put a GPS tracker on a TV commercial,' Schaefer wrote. 'When someone sees an ad about Pensacola and books a room, we don't know if they're staying on the beach or downtown.'

What Happens Next

The TDC board will begin its FY 2027 budget process in August. Early projections from the county's budget office anticipate flat or slightly declining collections, reflecting softening travel demand nationally and hurricane recovery concerns regionally.

Pensacola Beach business owners say they plan to attend the August meeting in force.

'We're not saying shut off the money to downtown. We're saying look at the roads, look at the drainage, look at the infrastructure that makes the whole thing work,' Caffey said. 'The beach is the engine. You have to maintain the engine.'

Peacock, the TDC chairman, said he welcomes public input.

'Every stakeholder has a voice in this process. That's how it's supposed to work,' he said. 'But at the end of the day, we have to make decisions that benefit the entire county's tourism economy. That's what we were appointed to do.'

The bed tax will keep flowing, one pillow at a time. The argument over where it lands is far from settled.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Crane Count: Downtown Pensacola Has 11 Active Construction Sites. Here's What's Coming.
articles.dek: From the Hashtag site to West Main, a building boom is reshaping the skyline. We mapped every project, tracked the timelines, and asked who's buying.
brief: Eleven major construction projects are currently active within a 12-block radius of downtown Pensacola, representing over $340 million in combined investment.
The building boom includes four mixed-use developments, three residential towers, two hotel projects, and two commercial renovations, with completion dates ranging from late 2026 to early 2028.
Local real estate agents report strong pre-sale activity from out-of-state buyers, particularly retirees from the Northeast and remote workers from Atlanta and Nashville.
articles.body:
Stand at the corner of Palafox and Garden on any weekday morning and count the cranes. There are three visible from this spot alone. Turn west toward the water and catch two more. The percussion of pile drivers has become downtown Pensacola's new soundtrack.

Eleven major construction projects are now active within a 12-block radius of the city's historic core. The Flightline spent three weeks mapping every site, pulling permits from Escambia County records, interviewing developers, and tracking sales data. What emerged is a portrait of a downtown in the middle of its most significant transformation since the urban renewal projects of the 1970s—though this time, the wrecking balls are largely staying home.

The Projects

The largest site by footprint sits at the former Hashtag location on South Palafox, where Atlanta-based Portman Holdings broke ground in February on a 14-story mixed-use tower. The $78 million project will include 186 residential units, 12,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and a rooftop restaurant. Completion is scheduled for March 2028.

"We looked at this market for three years before committing," said Daniel Kirby, Portman's regional development director, in a phone interview. "The demographics shifted. You have retirees who want walkability. You have remote workers who don't need to be in Atlanta or Birmingham anymore. Pensacola checked boxes it didn't check five years ago."

Three blocks north, the skeletal frame of the Aragon Residences rises above West Romana Street. The 11-story, 94-unit condominium project from local developer Gulf South Partners represents a $52 million investment. Sales began in January 2025, and according to listing agent Maria Fontaine of Berkshire Hathaway, 71 of the units are under contract.

"We've sold to buyers from 14 states," Fontaine said. "New York, New Jersey, Ohio—people who visited on vacation and decided they wanted to live here. We've also seen significant interest from Mobile and New Orleans. People trading up in quality of life."

The other active residential projects include:

  • The Belmont on Main (West Main Street): 8 stories, 62 units, $34 million. Developer: Coastal Equity Partners, Mobile. Completion: November 2026.
  • Palafox Lofts Phase II (South Palafox): 6 stories, 48 units, $28 million. Developer: Studer Properties, Pensacola. Completion: February 2027.
  • Bayfront Tower (South Baylen Street): 12 stories, 108 units, $61 million. Developer: Kolter Group, Palm Beach. Completion: August 2027.

Hotels Return

Two hotel projects mark a renewed bet on downtown tourism after the sector contracted during the pandemic years.

On East Government Street, a Marriott Tribute Portfolio property is rising on the site of the former Escambia County tax collector's office, which the county sold in 2024 for $3.2 million. The 142-room boutique hotel, developed by Naples-based Barron Collier Companies, carries a $47 million price tag and a December 2027 target opening.

Four blocks west, the long-stalled Southtowne hotel project has finally resumed construction after a two-year pause caused by financing disputes. Birmingham developer Harbert Realty Services acquired the partially completed structure in September 2025 and is converting it to an independent lifestyle hotel with 98 rooms. Opening is now projected for spring 2027.

"The first attempt was probably too ambitious for the moment," said Harbert spokesman Cole Morrison. "We right-sized the project. The bones were good. The location is still excellent."

Commercial and Mixed-Use

The remaining projects reflect downtown's evolution toward a live-work-play density that city planners have pursued for two decades.

At Jefferson and Baylen, the four-story Old City Market development will combine 22,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space with 34 apartments above. Developer 5eleven Group, based in Pensacola, describes it as an "urban food hall concept" with space for eight vendors and a central bar. Construction began in April; completion is expected in September 2027.

On West Intendencia Street, a historic three-story warehouse is being converted into creative office space by local investment group Wentworth Capital. The $8 million renovation will preserve the 1920s brick facade while adding modern infrastructure. Anchor tenant Saltmarsh, Cleaveland & Gund, a regional accounting firm, has pre-leased 60% of the building.

Finally, two smaller renovation projects round out the count: a $4 million conversion of a former bank building on East Garden Street into medical offices, and a $3.5 million buildout of ground-floor retail on South Tarragona.

Who's Buying?

Pre-sale data from the residential projects reveals a buyer profile that would have been uncommon a decade ago.

According to figures provided by listing agents and developers, roughly 60% of committed buyers at the Aragon, Belmont, and Bayfront projects are from out of state. The median age is 58. The majority are purchasing units as primary residences rather than vacation homes or investment properties.

"This isn't speculative condo-flipping," said Robert Ash, a broker with Levin Rinke Realty who has tracked downtown development for 15 years. "These are people who are actually moving here. They're selling houses in Connecticut or Illinois and buying in Pensacola. That's different from what we saw in the mid-2000s."

Prices reflect the shift. At the Aragon, one-bedroom units start at $425,000. Two-bedrooms range from $575,000 to $740,000. Penthouses have topped $1.2 million. At the Portman project, pricing has not been finalized, but marketing materials suggest units will start around $500,000.

Whether local wages can support these prices remains an open question. Escambia County's median household income in 2025 was $58,400, according to Census estimates—well below what would typically qualify a buyer for a $500,000 mortgage.

"These buildings aren't really being built for the existing Pensacola population," acknowledged Fontaine. "They're being built for people who are coming here with equity from other markets. That's the reality of what's happening."

Infrastructure Pressure

The building boom has prompted questions about whether downtown infrastructure can absorb the growth.

The 11 projects currently under construction will add roughly 500 residential units and 240 hotel rooms to a downtown core that currently contains approximately 1,200 housing units. That represents a 40% increase in downtown housing stock within two years.

Pensacola City Council member Teniadé Broughton, whose District 6 includes downtown, said she has raised infrastructure concerns with city staff.

"Parking is the obvious one," Broughton said. "But it's also stormwater. It's pedestrian safety. We're adding thousands of people to streets that were designed for a different era. I want to make sure we're planning ahead, not just reacting."

City administrator Keith Wilkins said in an email that the city has commissioned a downtown mobility study to assess impacts from current and projected development. Results are expected in October.

"We're aware of the growth and we're planning accordingly," Wilkins wrote. "Downtown development is a net positive for the city's tax base and economic vitality. Our job is to manage it responsibly."

The View From Street Level

At Constant Coffee on North Palafox, owner Dina Walsh has watched the construction spread block by block over the past three years. Her shop sits between two active sites.

"Honestly? It's loud," Walsh said on a recent Thursday, as a concrete truck rumbled past the window. "I've lost some morning regulars who got tired of the detours. But I'm not complaining. More people living downtown means more people walking past my door. I'm playing the long game."

Three doors south, real estate attorney Mark Castellanos offered a more tempered view.

"I've been here since 1994," he said. "I've seen boom and bust. The question isn't whether these buildings get built. The question is whether Pensacola can sustain the growth without losing what made people want to come here in the first place. That's the thing nobody knows yet."

Outside, another crane swung a load of rebar into position. The hammering resumed. The skyline kept changing.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Begins With New Flight Path Over Gulf Breeze
articles.dek: The Navy's demonstration squadron returns from the road for their signature Pensacola Beach show. This year's practice runs take a different route—and some residents noticed.
brief: Blue Angels practice flights this week are using an adjusted route that takes jets over the Gulf Breeze mainland rather than exclusively over Santa Rosa Sound
The Navy cites airspace coordination with Pensacola International Airport as the reason for the temporary change
Residents near Tiger Point reported low-altitude passes Monday morning, with some describing it as the loudest flyover activity they've experienced
articles.body:
The rumble hit Gulf Breeze at 11:47 a.m. Monday. Six F/A-18 Super Hornets in tight formation came in low over Pensacola Bay, banked hard, and roared directly over the Publix on Gulf Breeze Parkway. Car alarms went off in the parking lot. A woman dropped her phone.

This is homecoming week for the Blue Angels, the Navy's flight demonstration squadron based at Naval Air Station Pensacola. The team returns from their spring tour for the annual Pensacola Beach Air Show, scheduled for Friday and Saturday. But this year's practice runs are taking an unfamiliar route—one that's putting the jets directly over residential areas that usually only catch them from a distance.

"I've lived here nine years. They've never come over like that," said Marcus Delgado, who was washing his truck in his driveway on Oakmont Drive when the formation passed. "It was incredible. Also scared the hell out of my dog."

A Different Route

According to a Navy spokesman at NAS Pensacola, the adjusted flight path stems from temporary airspace coordination with Pensacola International Airport. Construction on Runway 17/35 has shifted commercial traffic patterns through Wednesday, requiring the Blue Angels to modify their practice box.

"The demonstration area remains centered over Pensacola Beach," said Lt. Cmdr. Brian Abe, the squadron's public affairs officer. "What's changed is the ingress and egress routes. We're working with FAA and the airport to ensure safe separation from commercial traffic."

The result: jets that typically approach from over the Sound or the open Gulf are now coming in from the north, crossing the Gulf Breeze mainland before reaching the beach. The standard practice show includes multiple high-speed passes, vertical climbs, and the signature Diamond 360 maneuver—all of which require approach corridors that extend well beyond the beach itself.

Abe said the modified routes will remain in place through Thursday's final practice session. The Friday and Saturday shows will use standard patterns, assuming the runway work finishes on schedule.

Tiger Point Takes the Noise

Residents in Tiger Point, the golf course community on the eastern end of Gulf Breeze, reported some of the most dramatic flyovers Monday. The neighborhood sits roughly three miles from the Pensacola Beach show center—close enough to hear the jets every year, but typically not directly beneath them.

Monday was different.

Jennifer Holt was on a work call in her home office when the first pass came through. "My Zoom froze because I think my whole house shook," she said. "My colleague asked if I was okay. I just said, 'Blue Angels.'"

Several residents posted videos to neighborhood Facebook groups showing the jets at what appeared to be unusually low altitude. One video, shot from a backyard on Plantation Drive, shows the six-jet Delta formation passing overhead with landing gear bays clearly visible.

Holt said she isn't complaining. "We moved here knowing NAS Pensacola was next door. This is part of the deal." But she noted the noise Monday was significantly louder than typical practice weeks. "Usually you hear them in the distance. This was in your chest."

The Airport Factor

Pensacola International Airport's Runway 17/35 has been undergoing a concrete rehabilitation project since late May. The work, part of a $12 million FAA-funded improvement package, requires periodic runway closures that push arriving and departing commercial flights onto Runway 8/26.

Airport spokesman David Schroeder confirmed the coordination with NAS Pensacola. "Anytime we have modified operations that affect our airspace, we work with the Navy and FAA to make sure everyone's operating safely," he said. "The Blue Angels practice week required some additional planning this year."

Schroeder said the runway work remains on track for completion by midweek, meaning Friday's air show should proceed without airspace complications.

Commercial traffic at Pensacola International was light Monday, with no significant delays reported. The airport handled 14 arrivals and 16 departures between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., according to FlightAware data.

What to Expect

Practice sessions continue through Thursday. The Navy schedules practice flights for late morning, typically beginning around 11:30 a.m., though exact timing depends on weather and operational factors. Each practice runs approximately 45 minutes and mirrors the full air show routine.

The Pensacola Beach Air Show itself is free to the public. Friday's show begins at 2 p.m. with civilian aerobatic acts, with the Blue Angels taking the sky at approximately 3 p.m. Saturday follows the same schedule.

Casino Beach and the surrounding area will be closed to vehicle traffic beginning Thursday evening. The Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce estimates 150,000 to 200,000 spectators attend over the two-day event, though crowd counts are unofficial.

For Gulf Breeze residents under the new flight path, the week offers an unexpectedly close look at the homecoming tradition. Delgado said he plans to set up a lawn chair in his driveway for Tuesday's practice.

"Might as well enjoy it," he said. "They're not going to be this close again."
